doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Playing for the audience and the state of jazz festivals
summary: Musicians owe the audience who paid; festivals now headline non-jazz acts, and jazz gets little media exposure.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: I’ve often wondered what would happen at one of these jazz parties if somebody announced, “okay, now we’re going to do an original composition.”

Well we have that in Five Play, our quintet here, we do some different kinds of arrangements. But we can’t, we wouldn’t do it. And the other thing that, even though musicians are artists, and they certainly are, but you have to remember the only reason you’re on the stage is because there’s an audience there. They paid money to see you. You owe them something. And the audience would owe us respect to present something that they like but you have to know where you’re going and gauge your program towards that. And I love playing “Take the A Train,” and I love just swinging and I love playing stuff that’s a little weirder too. But you just have to know who you’re playing for, and hope not to, it’s like that’s the business part. You have to pay attention to it.

And I don’t know how to educate audiences to, you know, you must like this new kind of harmony, or that kind of thing, like to get people to like that. Because the diversity between a festival like this and some of the — well now you can’t even really count some of the festivals as jazz festivals because the headliners will be James Brown and Earth Wind & Fire, things that have nothing to do with jazz at all but they’ve become just big music festivals just to keep the crowd interested. And again it’s a whole trickle down system of what the record company and the media promotes, and what people hear on the radio all the time. If there were more jazz stations — like my nieces and nephews, they never would hear jazz if they didn’t come to my — I see them at concerts and they’re falling asleep by the third song, but they don’t even have a chance to hear it. Like if it was in people’s faces more, if you drove by and saw a billboard with the Count Basie band instead of Ricky Martin or something. You know, if people were just aware of it more then I think they might have an interest in seeing the concerts.
